heuristics.rule: Never give a number first — always redirect to their budget range
heuristics.condition: When a recruiter asks for your salary expectations or current compensation before an offer is made...
heuristics.action: ...deflect with enthusiasm and ask what the budgeted range is for the role
heuristics.because: Their number is almost always more useful than anchoring with yours — you risk leaving money on the table or pricing yourself out unnecessarily

heuristics.rule: Never accept or reject a verbal offer on the spot
heuristics.condition: When a recruiter delivers a verbal offer during a call...
heuristics.action: ...express enthusiasm, request the formal written offer, and set a 24–48 hour review window
heuristics.because: You need time to compare to market data and the act of reviewing is not a negotiation — it creates no friction while buying you leverage time

heuristics.rule: Give a specific number, not a range, when countering
heuristics.condition: When making a counter-offer on salary...
heuristics.action: ...state one precise target number rather than a range
heuristics.because: Ranges anchor at the low end — the company will interpret a range as permission to offer the bottom of it

heuristics.rule: Express genuine enthusiasm before making any ask
heuristics.action: ...lead with specific, sincere excitement about the role before naming your number
heuristics.because: Enthusiasm signals good faith and keeps the tone collaborative rather than adversarial, which makes the recruiter more willing to advocate for you internally

heuristics.rule: After giving your number, stop talking
heuristics.condition: When you have just stated your counter number in a negotiation...
heuristics.action: ...remain silent and let the recruiter respond
heuristics.because: The discomfort of silence belongs to the recruiter, not you — filling it weakens your position by inviting you to walk back your ask

heuristics.rule: Always ask about the signing bonus as a separate lever, even after 'best and final'
heuristics.condition: When a company says the base salary cannot move due to band constraints...
heuristics.action: ...pivot explicitly to signing bonus as an alternative lever
heuristics.because: Signing bonuses come from a different budget, don't affect payroll or salary bands, and companies frequently have flexibility there even when base is locked

heuristics.rule: Negotiate on the phone, confirm in writing
heuristics.condition: When a recruiter is handling negotiations over email...
heuristics.action: ...request a 15-minute phone call before responding with any specific counter
heuristics.because: Recruiters batch and can easily decline email negotiations; on a live call they are actively advocating for you in real time, which is where movement actually happens

heuristics.rule: Counter one ask at a time, not five simultaneously
heuristics.condition: When you have multiple things you want to negotiate...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize and sequence your asks rather than stacking them all at once
heuristics.because: Simultaneous asks feel like demands, create friction, and reduce the recruiter's ability to say yes to anything — sequencing keeps momentum

heuristics.rule: Offer to sign today when you're close to your number
heuristics.condition: When the negotiation is near resolution and you're close to an acceptable number...
heuristics.action: ...explicitly offer to sign the same day if they can reach your final number
heuristics.because: It creates urgency on their side while signaling you are negotiating in good faith and not stringing them along

heuristics.rule: Frame a deadline extension request around decision quality, not personal need
heuristics.condition: When facing an exploding offer with a tight deadline...
heuristics.action: ...request more time by invoking that a confident, thoughtful decision benefits both parties
heuristics.because: Companies have invested 10–20 hours interviewing you and don't want to lose you over a few days — framing around decision quality is harder to refuse than 'I need more time'

heuristics.rule: Get every verbal commitment in the offer letter before signing
heuristics.condition: When a company agrees in principle to a signing bonus or non-cash benefit during negotiation...
heuristics.action: ...explicitly ask for it to be written into the offer letter before you sign
heuristics.because: 'We'll figure it out later' is not a commitment — verbal agreements before signing have no enforceability

heuristics.rule: Align on compensation before formally accepting a promotion, not after
heuristics.condition: When a manager announces you are being promoted...
heuristics.action: ...ask about the comp adjustment before expressing full acceptance of the new role
heuristics.because: Once you've visibly accepted the promotion, your leverage to negotiate the associated comp drops significantly

decision_factors.factor: Whether you have a competing offer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A competing offer transforms negotiation from a one-sided ask into a bilateral decision the company must respond to — it provides concrete external validation of your market value
decision_factors.how_to_assess: You either have one or you don't — if you do, know the exact number and timeline attached to it before using it as leverage

decision_factors.factor: Whether the negotiation is happening by phone or email
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Phone calls put recruiters in real-time advocacy mode; email allows easy, low-friction 'no' responses and loses nuance
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess the channel being used — if email, proactively request a call before counter-offering

decision_factors.factor: Whether the base salary band is actually locked
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If base truly cannot move, knowing this quickly redirects your energy to signing bonus, equity, or non-cash levers that have real budget flexibility
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask HR directly whether the band is the constraint; test by asking about signing bonus separately even after being told base is final

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Vague asks ('something closer to $200K') anchor less effectively than precise numbers ('I'm looking for $195K') — precision signals market research and confidence
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Before negotiating, research the role on levels.fyi or equivalent sources and commit to a single specific number

decision_factors.factor: Timing of the ask relative to offer stage
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Giving a number before an offer is made anchors you downward; negotiating only after receiving the written offer maximizes leverage
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Track whether you are pre-offer, post-verbal-offer, or post-written-offer — each stage has a different appropriate script

decision_factors.why_it_matters: In states with salary history bans, you have legal cover to refuse sharing current compensation, removing a key pressure tactic recruiters use
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Know whether your state has a salary history ban before any recruiter call; your deflection script differs depending on this

decision_factors.factor: Whether non-cash levers are on the table
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Remote work arrangements, in-office day counts, and other non-cash terms have real life impact and are often more negotiable than base salary
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Scan the offer letter for what is unspecified — unspecified terms are open negotiation opportunities

decision_factors.why_it_matters: An exploding offer compresses your ability to gather competing offers and make comparisons — extensions are almost always negotiable but require proactive action
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Note the stated deadline and immediately assess whether you need more time; the sooner you request an extension, the more reasonable it appears

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating over email instead of requesting a phone call
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Recruiter can respond with a templated 'no' in seconds with no social friction — the path of least resistance is always to decline in writing
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who are conflict-averse and prefer written communication, believing it is more comfortable or professional

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Giving a salary range instead of a single number when counter-offering
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The company anchors to the bottom of your range and treats it as your actual ask, not a midpoint
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who believe showing flexibility signals reasonableness — it actually signals willingness to accept the lower number

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Expressing full enthusiasm for a promotion before discussing compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You implicitly signal acceptance of the role under any terms, eliminating your negotiating leverage before comp is even discussed
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers who are excited and grateful for recognition and lead with emotion before thinking strategically

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a verbal commitment on signing bonus or remote work without written confirmation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The commitment has no legal enforceability and the specific person who made it may not be around when you join
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who build trust-based relationships with recruiters and assume goodwill will carry through to onboarding

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: It signals that no single concession will close the deal, which reduces recruiter motivation to push internally for any of them
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Analytically-minded candidates who want to optimize everything at once and believe comprehensive asks are efficient

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not asking for an extension on an exploding offer deadline
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You make a consequential financial decision without adequate market comparison data, and implicitly accept terms that may have been improvable with one more competing offer
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who fear appearing difficult or non-committal, especially those who are relieved to have any offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Giving a number first when asked for salary expectations pre-offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Social pressure in the moment makes silence or deflection feel rude; candidates assume they must answer the question directly
failure_patterns.consequence: You anchor the entire negotiation at or below your stated number — the company has no reason to offer more than what you said you expected
warning_signs: You feel obligated to answer every recruiter question directly
You give a range 'to seem flexible' before you have any offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting or declining a verbal offer on the spot
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Emotional response to good news triggers immediate acceptance; or anxiety about seeming indecisive triggers quick response
failure_patterns.consequence: You lose the window to do market research and negotiate from a position of information rather than gratitude or panic
warning_signs: You say 'yes' or signal strong acceptance during the call where the offer is delivered
You ask no clarifying questions when the offer is presented

failure_patterns.pattern: Folding after the first 'this is our best and final offer'
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The phrase sounds definitive and candidates interpret it as a true hard stop rather than a negotiating position
failure_patterns.consequence: You leave money on the table — signing bonus and other levers often remain available even when base is genuinely capped
warning_signs: You treat 'best and final' as equivalent to 'nothing else is possible'
You never ask about signing bonus after being told base cannot move

failure_patterns.pattern: Paralysis in the moment — knowing you should negotiate but not knowing the words
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates understand the principle but have no rehearsed scripts, so anxiety in the moment prevents execution
failure_patterns.consequence: Either no negotiation happens at all, or the ask is framed poorly and creates unnecessary friction without achieving movement
warning_signs: You have researched market data but still say nothing when the offer comes
You plan to negotiate 'if the number feels low' but have no script prepared

failure_patterns.pattern: Conducting all negotiation over email when a phone call would be more effective
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Email feels safer, less confrontational, and gives candidates time to craft responses carefully
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiters can batch-process and decline easily in writing; live advocacy and real-time movement almost never happen over email
warning_signs: You have never asked to move the negotiation to a phone call
You respond to offer details in the same email thread they were sent in

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a competing offer, and if so, what is the exact number and deadline?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have external leverage to use — a competing offer fundamentally changes the negotiation dynamic and the scripts available to you
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is it from a company the hiring company would consider a credible competitor, and are you willing to name it?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What market data do you have from sources like levels.fyi that can serve as a proxy for external validation?

diagnostic_questions.question: At what stage are you — pre-offer, post-verbal-offer, or post-written-offer?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Which phase of negotiation strategy applies — deflection scripts, time-buying scripts, or active counter scripts are each stage-specific
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If post-written-offer: have you identified every unspecified term in the letter that could be negotiated?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If pre-offer: are you being asked for salary expectations, and do you know whether your state has a salary history ban?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the negotiation happening by phone or email?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have real-time advocacy from the recruiter or whether you're getting batched, low-friction responses
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If phone: have you prepared your specific number and practiced the silence after delivering it?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If email: have you requested a 15-minute call before submitting any counter?

diagnostic_questions.question: Has the recruiter said 'this is best and final' — and have you asked about signing bonus separately?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you've exhausted only one lever (base) or tested all available ones — signing bonus often has a different budget and different answer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If you asked about signing bonus and were also told no: are there non-cash terms like remote work or start date that still haven't been addressed?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you haven't asked about signing bonus yet: what specific amount would bridge the gap between the current offer and your target?

diagnostic_questions.question: For a promotion: did you discuss compensation before or after expressing acceptance of the new role?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether your leverage has already been spent — accepting the role emotionally before negotiating comp eliminates your primary bargaining chip
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If before: what market data do you have for the new title to anchor your counter?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If after: is there still an opening to reframe the conversation as 'aligning before we finalize' rather than renegotiating after acceptance?

industry_realities.common_belief: Exploding offer deadlines are firm and non-negotiable
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most exploding offer deadlines are negotiable — companies have invested 10–20 hours interviewing a candidate and will not lose them over a 3–7 day extension
industry_realities.implication: Always request an extension framed around making a confident decision; treat the deadline as a starting position, not a hard constraint

industry_realities.common_belief: 'This is our best and final offer' means there is nothing left to negotiate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Base salary band may genuinely be locked, but signing bonus often comes from a completely different budget and may still have flexibility even after 'best and final'
industry_realities.implication: After hearing 'best and final,' pivot specifically to signing bonus before accepting or walking away

industry_realities.common_belief: Negotiating aggressively will make you seem difficult and cost you the offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: Enthusiastic, specific, collaborative counter-offers are expected by recruiters — the scripts that work are not adversarial; they are good-faith conversations
industry_realities.implication: Tone and framing matter more than the act of negotiating — enthusiasm before any ask is not a tactic, it is what makes the ask land well

industry_realities.common_belief: Email is a professional and effective channel for salary negotiation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Recruiters can batch and decline email negotiations with minimal friction — live phone calls are where real advocacy and movement happen
industry_realities.implication: Proactively request a phone call before submitting any counter-offer, even if the entire process has been conducted via email

industry_realities.common_belief: Giving a salary range signals flexibility and makes you easier to work with
industry_realities.actual_reality: Ranges anchor at the low end — the company treats the bottom of your range as your actual ask and has no incentive to offer more
industry_realities.implication: Always give one specific number when counter-offering, never a range

industry_realities.common_belief: Unspecified terms in an offer letter will be worked out after you join
industry_realities.actual_reality: Terms that are not in the offer letter are not commitments — verbal agreements made during recruitment have no enforceability after you sign
industry_realities.implication: Any agreed-upon term — signing bonus, remote work arrangement, in-office day count — must be in the written offer letter before you sign

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Response to recruiter salary questions pre-offer
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Answers directly with a number or range, believing it is rude or evasive to deflect
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Deflects with enthusiasm and redirects to the company's budgeted range, understanding that the first number sets the ceiling
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Giving your number first anchors the entire negotiation downward — seniors understand that information asymmetry at this stage is entirely in the company's favor

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Responds emotionally with excitement or relief, sometimes accepting on the spot or signaling strong acceptance
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Expresses genuine enthusiasm while immediately establishing a review window, treating the verbal offer as the start of a process
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Accepting on the spot eliminates all negotiating leverage; seniors know that a short review window is both expected and costless

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats 'best and final' as the true end of negotiation and either accepts or declines without probing other levers
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Acknowledges 'best and final' on base salary but immediately pivots to signing bonus as a separate budget lever
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Seniors understand that 'best and final' on base does not mean 'best and final on everything' — signing bonuses are structurally different and frequently still available

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Uses vague language like 'something in the $190s' or gives a range to seem flexible
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: States one precise number — 'I'm looking for $195,000' — after researching market data from a named source
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Precision signals preparation, confidence, and market awareness; vagueness signals uncertainty and invites the company to anchor at the low end

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Conducts negotiation by email because it feels safer and allows more time to craft responses
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Proactively requests a phone call before counter-offering, knowing that real-time advocacy is where movement happens
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Email creates a low-friction path to 'no'; phone calls require the recruiter to engage in real time and advocate internally on your behalf

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Expresses excitement and gratitude for the promotion announcement before asking about compensation
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Asks about compensation before signaling full acceptance, framing it as wanting to start the next chapter aligned
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Expressing acceptance before negotiating comp permanently reduces leverage — the company has already achieved their goal of getting you to take the role
